clue.text: Flatulence of cricket team beginning to subside around November

indicators.note: around means the other letters go round the one for November

parts.note: the Windies is the nickname of the West Indies cricket team
N is November in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of subside

explanation.surface: A cricket side's gassy problem starts to ease around November.
explanation.walkthrough: The Windies (the West Indies cricket team) plus S, the beginning of 'subside', go around N.
explanation.definitionFit: Windiness is the state of having wind, gas in the gut, which is what flatulence means.

clue.text: County flags

definitions.note: The S here belongs to a county's standard abbreviation rather than making a plural, so a singular definition sits fairly beside a verb reading.
definitions.meaning: the recognised short form of Wiltshire, as written on an address
a plant that flags is drooping for want of water, and so is a flagging spirit

explanation.walkthrough: Two words, two definitions, no wordplay at all — and the trap is 'flags', which reads as bunting on a county show stall rather than as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: County -> WILTS: the accepted abbreviation for Wiltshire; flags -> WILTS: a plant losing turgor droops, and enthusiasm that flags sags the same way.

clue.text: Things struggling with fossil fuel waste

indicators.note: something struggling is thrashing about and will not hold still, so its letters do not stay where they were put

parts.note: the six letters of this word are the material to be rearranged
oil is the fossil fuel that is drilled rather than mined

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fossil fuel waste' hangs together far too well as a phrase, and that is the trap: only the first two words of it belong to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: waste -> NIGHT SOIL: night soil is the old term for human excrement carted away after dark, so it is waste in the most literal sense.

clue.text: Reportedly, I adore residents of Battersea, part of London

indicators.note: what is reported is spoken rather than written, and the match asked for is a run-together of speech, not an exact pairing of sounds

parts.note: to adore is to love, and said at speed those two words come out as two quite different ones
the home in Battersea has been taking in strays of the barking kind since 1860

explanation.walkthrough: The whole surface is one fond sentence about animal rescue, and it has to be said out loud before it turns into a place on the Thames.
explanation.definitionFit: part of London -> ISLE OF DOGS: the Thames peninsula in Tower Hamlets, now dominated by Canary Wharf — named here by category, not by name.

clue.text: Times regularly queried showing synth-pop duo

parts.note: an era is a stretch of history, so eras are times

indicators.note: at regular intervals means every second one, so you count off alternate letters and let the rest go

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of the word, in that order

explanation.walkthrough: The italics point at the newspaper and the capital is the surface's doing; the word is wanted as a plain noun meaning ages.
explanation.definitionFit: synth-pop duo -> ERASURE: definition by example, since Vince Clarke and Andy Bell's band is one such duo rather than the class of them.

clue.text: Family stopping small cat doing unhealthy activity

parts.note: S is the label on the smallest shirt in the pile

indicators.note: to stop somewhere is to lodge there for a while, so this word takes up residence inside the other

parts.note: a mog, or moggie, is an ordinary household cat
your kin are your family, near and distant

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a cat with an unfortunate habit. Mechanically, MOG is the crossword's standing three-letter cat, worth filing alongside TOM and PUSS.
explanation.definitionFit: doing unhealthy activity -> SMOKING: the -ing form names the act of using tobacco, the textbook example of a habit that damages health.

clue.text: Premise of large book set in Highbury

parts.note: L is the clothing size and the standard short form of large
Jane Austen's novel is set in the village of Highbury

explanation.walkthrough: Highbury is a real corner of north London as well as Austen's invented village, and the surface leans on the football ground to keep you off the bookshelf.
explanation.definitionFit: Premise -> LEMMA: in logic a lemma is a subsidiary proposition proved on the way to a theorem, so it functions as a stepping-stone assumption.

clue.text: Accumulate boomerangs in circle

indicators.note: a boomerang is thrown out and comes straight back, so the word it marks is read from its far end

parts.note: to pool money or effort is to gather it into a common store

explanation.walkthrough: 'Boomerangs in circle' reads as a picture of Australia while doing two jobs at once: naming the turn, and in 'circle' giving the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: circle -> LOOP: a loop is a line that comes round to meet itself, which is a circle in the loose everyday sense rather than the geometer's.

clue.text: Crop cloth covering snooker table, with money to replace balls, at first

indicators.note: to replace signals a swap: one letter goes in where another comes out

parts.note: baize is the green felt stretched over a snooker table

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter of the word balls

parts.note: the word whose opening letter is taken

explanation.surface: A snooker hall is refitted: new cloth, and cash spent on fresh balls.
explanation.walkthrough: Take BAIZE; 'balls, at first' is B, and money (M) is put 'to replace' it.
explanation.definitionFit: This cereal plant, also called corn, is one of the world's major farmed grains.

clue.text: Negative critique of creative work regarding skilled worker

parts.note: painting, sculpture and the rest are creative work
the sour verdict itself, spelled out as a flat statement that the thing is obsessively fussy

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer three ways and it becomes a critic's dismissal of a whole gallery. The sneer and the craftsman's adjective are spelt with the same nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: regarding skilled worker -> ARTISANAL: the adjective formed from artisan, a craftsman working by hand, now stamped on bread and cheese to promise exactly that.

clue.text: Allowed actor initially to enter stage left

indicators.note: to enter tells us the actor's letter goes inside the stage-and-left pair

parts.note: a stage of a journey is a leg

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of actor only

parts.note: its first letter is A

explanation.surface: A theatre note: an actor was permitted to come on from stage left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stage left' reads as a theatre direction, but stage is LEG and left is L; 'initially' takes A from actor, and 'to enter' slips it between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Something allowed by law is legal: a straightforward synonym meaning permitted.

clue.text: A game point for champion

parts.note: the clue's own opening word, used exactly as it stands
polo is the game played on horseback with mallets
the gist of an argument is its essential point

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a scoreboard, three words that belong together in a racket sport; underneath, none of them has anything to do with the others.
explanation.definitionFit: champion -> APOLOGIST: an apologist argues in defence of a doctrine or person, championing a cause in print rather than in a contest.

clue.text: Noted work?

definitions.meaning: the surface reading is the adjective: celebrated, distinguished, the sort of thing people have heard of
the setter's reading needs a piece of writing, and the question mark warns that 'noted' is about to change sense

explanation.walkthrough: There is nothing to take apart here. The whole clue is one definition read twice, and the pun is on notes as marks on a stave rather than fame.
explanation.definitionFit: Noted work? -> SET TO MUSIC: a poem handed to a composer has had notes put to it, so it becomes 'noted' in the literal, musical sense.

clue.text: Starting late, foreigners bypassing one French city

indicators.note: begin the word later than it begins itself, and its own opening letter is left behind
to bypass a place is to go round without entering it, so that letter is passed over

parts.note: aliens are foreigners in the immigration officer's vocabulary
one is I in Roman numerals, and it is the letter passed over

explanation.walkthrough: Two subtractions in a row is unusual, and both instructions read as ordinary travel English — starting late, bypassing somewhere — which is exactly why they hide.
explanation.definitionFit: French city -> LENS: definition by example — Lens is the old mining town in the Pas-de-Calais, best known now for its football club.

clue.text: European chap worried about withdrawn photo's release

indicators.note: about means going round, so the European-chap-worried string wraps the reversed photo

parts.note: a chap is a man
worried as in 'what's eating you?' gives ATE, past tense of eat

indicators.note: withdrawn means pulled back, so the word for photo is read backwards

parts.note: a pic is a photo

explanation.surface: A European man frets over a retracted photograph being published.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Withdrawn' reverses the photo word, and 'about' has European, chap and worried wrap round it; worried is ATE, as in 'what's eating you?'.
explanation.definitionFit: To emancipate is to set free, so it is a verb meaning to release from bondage or restriction.

clue.text: Perhaps Declan Donnelly content to scavenge or diet

indicators.note: the content of something is what sits inside it, so the letters wanted are already there in the words that follow

parts.note: seven consecutive letters run straight across the two word breaks in this phrase

explanation.walkthrough: Declan Donnelly is the Dec of Ant and Dec, who was born and raised in Newcastle upon Tyne. A Geordie is the nickname for anyone from Tyneside, so he is one example of a Geordie; 'Perhaps' says the clue gives an example, not a synonym. The letters run across scaven(GE OR DIE)t.
explanation.definitionFit: Perhaps Declan Donnelly -> GEORDIE: a Geordie is a person from Newcastle or Tyneside (it is not his name). Dec is one, so this is a definition by example, flagged by 'Perhaps'.

clue.text: Have to stop game in river

indicators.note: to stop somewhere is to break your journey and stay there, so this word halts inside the other

parts.note: grouse is the game bird shot on moors from the twelfth of August
to have lunch is to eat it

explanation.walkthrough: Grouse is worth filing away: 'game' in a crossword is almost always either a bird or a three-letter sport, and both readings sit in this surface.
explanation.definitionFit: river -> GREAT OUSE: the Great Ouse runs from Northamptonshire to the Wash, so the definition names it by category and leaves you the name.

clue.text: Match tactics having quietly ignored SE Asian players

definitions.note: The answer is a single ensemble, so a plural definition names it by the musicians in it — the same licence that lets 'players' define an orchestra.

parts.note: a match and a game are the same fixture

indicators.note: to ignore something is to leave it out altogether, so the letter named never reaches the grid

parts.note: a plan is the tactics settled on before kick-off
piano, marked p on a score, is the instruction to play quietly

explanation.walkthrough: Football all the way through the surface, and the answer is a Javanese percussion orchestra — the distance between the two is the whole pleasure of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: SE Asian players -> GAMELAN: the tuned-percussion orchestra of Java and Bali, so the definition names it by region and by what it is made of.

clue.text: Royal dorm upset Dick Whittington?

indicators.note: upsetting something tips it over and spills what was in it, so the letters land in a different order

parts.note: the nine letters of these two words are the whole of the material

explanation.walkthrough: Dick Whittington is a pantomime as well as a real fifteenth-century merchant, and 'Royal dorm' is the sort of phrase that only ever exists to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Dick Whittington? -> LORD MAYOR: definition by example, and the question mark says so — the pantomime hero turned again and ended up holding the office in London.

clue.text: Relating to acid derived from gall nuts put into melting ice

indicators.note: put into means the anagrammed gall goes inside the other letters
melting suggests the ice loses its shape, so its letters are rearranged
nuts, meaning crazy, signals that the letters of gall are jumbled

explanation.surface: A chemistry instruction: an acid made from gall nuts is added to thawing ice.
explanation.walkthrough: Ellagic acid really is made from gall nuts, which disguises 'nuts' as part of a botanical term when it is an anagram signal. 'Melting' scrambles the ice as well, and 'put into' sets the jumbled gall in the middle of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Ellagic is the adjective used for ellagic acid, a compound found in oak galls and tannins.

clue.text: Prove bit of negligence in two companies

indicators.note: in places the single letter within the two company words

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company and a firm is another company, giving CO and FIRM

indicators.note: a bit of negligence is just its first letter

parts.note: its first letter is N

explanation.surface: Showing a small amount of carelessness exists within two businesses.
explanation.walkthrough: The two companies are CO (the abbreviation) and FIRM; 'bit of' takes N from negligence, and 'in' puts it between them.
explanation.definitionFit: To confirm something is to establish its truth, a close synonym of prove.

clue.text: Army officer is common

definitions.meaning: the senior commissioned rank in an army, above a brigadier
the adjective for something widespread, as in a rule that holds everywhere

explanation.walkthrough: Four words and no wordplay: the clue is two meanings laid end to end, with 'is' doing the work of an equals sign between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Army officer -> GENERAL: the senior commissioned rank; common -> GENERAL: widespread or prevailing, as in general opinion, rather than common meaning vulgar.

clue.text: Scrambled eggs in back of van can be restorative

indicators.note: scrambling eggs breaks them up and stirs them together, which is exactly what happens to these letters

parts.note: the six letters of these two words are most of the material

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter, so only that one is taken from it

parts.note: the last letter of the word joins the rest of the fodder

explanation.walkthrough: A van with scrambled eggs in the back is a complete picture, and it is made entirely of letters — even the small word 'in' is fodder rather than joinery.
explanation.definitionFit: restorative -> GINSENG: the root is taken as a tonic in Chinese medicine, so 'restorative' is the herbalist's sense rather than a medical one.

clue.text: Pull close to station in Barnsley?

parts.note: to tow a caravan is to pull it

indicators.note: close here is the noun meaning an ending, so you want the letter the word closes with

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to station' reads as an estate agent's boast, which is the disguise; the question mark on Barnsley is the honest signal that it is only an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Barnsley? -> TOWN: definition by example — the South Yorkshire place is one, and the question mark admits it is an instance rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Shorebird is nameless stray

parts.note: cattle that stray wander off the pasture
N is the short form of name, and it is the letter dropped here

explanation.walkthrough: 'Nameless stray' is a sad little picture of a lost dog, and it is two instructions: a word meaning stray, with one letter of it taken out.
explanation.definitionFit: Shorebird -> WADER: waders are the long-legged birds — redshanks, avocets, curlews — that feed by wading in shallow water at the tide line.

clue.text: Awkwardly mention ear — it's one of a pair, the mirror image of the other

definitions.text: one of a pair, the mirror image of the other

indicators.note: doing a thing awkwardly is doing it clumsily, and letters handled clumsily come out in the wrong order

parts.note: the ten letters of these two words are exactly the material needed

explanation.walkthrough: An ear really is one of a mirrored pair, so fodder and definition are describing the same thing — a rare clue where the surface tells the truth twice.
explanation.definitionFit: one of a pair, the mirror image of the other -> ENANTIOMER: in chemistry, either of two molecules whose atoms are arranged as non-superimposable mirror images.

clue.text: Helping to release one in desert

indicators.note: releasing something is letting it go, so the letter named is set loose from the word holding it

parts.note: a helping is a measured share, which is what a ration is
one is I in Roman numerals, and it is the letter let go

explanation.walkthrough: Prison food on the surface, and underneath it is what one inmate does to another. 'Desert' is the verb here, so read it as abandon rather than as sand.
explanation.definitionFit: desert -> RAT ON: to rat on your friends is to betray and abandon them, the informer's version of deserting a cause.

clue.text: Lament almost lying about network

indicators.note: almost the whole word means all but the end of it, so the final letter never gets written
something left lying about has been tipped onto its side, and these letters are set down the other way round

parts.note: a dirge is a slow song of mourning, here docked of its last letter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Lying about' is doing two jobs at once: it is the instruction to turn the letters, and it keeps the surface's picture of clutter on the floor.
explanation.definitionFit: network -> GRID: the sense in 'the National Grid' — an interconnected network of cables or pipes, rather than a pattern of ruled squares.

clue.text: Weaken female leaving to provide finance for fur

indicators.note: what leaves a word is no longer in it, so the letter named walks out before the pieces are joined

parts.note: to fund a project is to provide the finance for it
F is the standard short form of female, and it is the letter that goes
ermine is the white winter coat of the stoat, worn on ceremonial robes

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a campaigning story about funding the fur trade, which is the sort of topical sentence that stops you counting letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Weaken -> UNDERMINE: literally to dig away what something stands on, and by extension to erode a person's authority or an argument's strength.

clue.text: So far, simple to cycle in front of Tesla

indicators.note: in front of places the cycled word before the next piece
to cycle a word is to move its first letter round to the end

parts.note: simple means easy
T is the symbol of the tesla, the SI unit of magnetic flux density

explanation.surface: Driving a Tesla is said to be easy compared with riding a bicycle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to cycle' moves the E of EASY to the back, giving ASYE, which goes 'in front of' T. Tesla is not the car but the physics unit.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means up to the present time, used of something that has not happened yet.

clue.text: Made a mistake about western wine

indicators.note: in an across answer, western means read right to left, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: re means about or concerning
red is a colour of wine

explanation.surface: Someone got it wrong about a wine from the West.
explanation.walkthrough: RE read 'western' is ER, then RED.
explanation.definitionFit: To err is to make a mistake, so erred is the past tense.

clue.text: Nursing officer welcoming revolutionary English microwave source

indicators.note: welcoming means taking in a guest, so the reversed piece goes inside

parts.note: a matron is a senior nurse in charge of a hospital ward

indicators.note: revolutionary suggests turning round, so the abbreviation is read backwards

parts.note: Eng. is the usual dictionary abbreviation of English

explanation.surface: A senior nurse makes a radical Englishman welcome on the ward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' turns ENG into GNE, and MATRON is 'welcoming' it after MA.
explanation.definitionFit: This vacuum tube generates the high-frequency radiation used in radar and in microwave ovens.
